segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, let us leave behind the basic message about Christ and be carried on to maturity, not laying again a foundation of turning back from dead works and of faith in God,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: instruction about washings and the laying on of hands, about the resurrection of the dead and eternal judgment.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And this we will do, if indeed God permits.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For it is impossible, when people have once been enlightened, have tasted the heavenly gift and become sharers in the Holy Spirit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and have tasted the good word of God and the powers of the coming age,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and then have fallen away, to renew them again to turning back, since they are crucifying the Son of God all over again for themselves and holding him up to public shame.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For ground that drinks the rain that often falls on it and bears a crop useful to those for whose sake it is farmed receives a share of blessing from God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if it produces thorns and thistles, it is worthless and close to being cursed, and its end is to be burned.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But about you, dear friends, we are convinced of better things, things that go with salvation, even though we speak this way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For God is not unjust; he will not forget your work and the love you showed for his name when you served the holy ones, as you still do.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We long for each of you to show the same eagerness for the full assurance of hope until the end,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that you may not become sluggish, but imitators of those who through faith and patience inherit the promises.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For when God made his promise to Abraham, since he had no one greater to swear by, he swore by himself,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: saying,

segments.speaker: God
segments.text: “I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so, after waiting patiently, Abraham obtained the promise.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For people swear by someone greater than themselves, and for them the oath, given as confirmation, is the end of every dispute.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So God, wanting to show even more clearly to the heirs of the promise how unchangeable his purpose was, guaranteed it with an oath,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that through two unchangeable things, in which it is impossible for God to lie, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope set before us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: We have this hope as an anchor of the soul, secure and firm, and it enters the inner place behind the curtain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: where Jesus has entered as a forerunner on our behalf, having become a high priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek.

notes.note: The traditional rendering is “repentance,” which most translations keep as an established term. In modern English that word centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek, echoing the prophets’ call to return to God, describes a change of direction in mind and conduct. Here it is a turning away “from dead works,” paired with faith directed toward God.

Older versions have “perfection”; most modern translations have “maturity,” which fits the contrast just drawn between infants on milk and adults on solid food (5:13–14). The word also belongs to a theme of “completeness” or “perfection” that runs through Hebrews, and some interpreters think that fuller sense is in view here as well.

A few early manuscripts read “instruction” in a form that sets it alongside “foundation,” so that the instruction about washings, laying on of hands, resurrection and judgment is itself the foundation; this is the reading translated. Most manuscripts read “of instruction,” making it one more item in the list of what the foundation consists of. The difference in meaning is slight.

Many translations have “baptisms.” The Greek word here is plural and is not the usual New Testament noun for Christian baptism; elsewhere it is used of Jewish ritual washings (Hebrews 9:10; Mark 7:4). The instruction probably concerned how Christian baptism differed from other purification rites, though the exact reference is uncertain.

notes.phrase: since they are crucifying the Son of God all over again
notes.note: Outside the New Testament this verb normally means simply “crucify,” but ancient Greek-speaking interpreters understood it here as “crucify again,” which suits the context and is followed by most translations. The clause can also be read as “while they are crucifying,” which would limit the impossibility to the time they persist in this stance. The scope of the warning in verses 4–6 is among the most debated questions in the letter.

The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep; others use “God’s people.” The word refers to all members of the community as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel, not to specially canonized or exceptionally virtuous individuals.

The Greek word can mean either complete certainty or complete fulfillment. On the second reading the author wants the readers’ eagerness to continue until their hope is fully realized. Most translations take it as assurance, as here.

notes.phrase: I will surely bless you, and I will surely multiply you.
notes.note: The quotation is from Genesis 22:17, where, after Abraham’s offering of Isaac, God says “By myself I have sworn” (Genesis 22:16). The Greek reads literally “blessing I will bless you and multiplying I will multiply you,” reproducing a Hebrew idiom of emphasis, and opens with a particle that marks a solemn oath.

The two things are generally understood to be God’s promise and the oath added to it. The author’s point is that either alone would be reliable, and the oath was added for the sake of the hearers’ confidence.

notes.phrase: to take hold of the hope set before us
notes.note: The Greek can be construed in two ways: “we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to take hold of the hope,” as here, or “we who have fled to take hold of the hope might have strong encouragement.” Translations are divided, and the overall sense differs little.

notes.phrase: the inner place behind the curtain
notes.note: The curtain separated the innermost room of the tabernacle, the Most Holy Place, from the rest of the sanctuary; only the high priest passed behind it, once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). The author uses it as an image of God’s own presence in heaven, which Jesus has entered.

notes.phrase: according to the order of Melchizedek
notes.note: The phrase comes from Psalm 110:4, “You are a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek,” already quoted at 5:6. Melchizedek is the priest-king of Salem who meets Abraham in Genesis 14:18–20. The verse returns to the subject broken off at 5:10 and introduces the extended argument of chapter 7.

candidates.reason: The vocative recurs throughout the letters and translators split between “beloved,” “dear friends” and “loved ones”; readers would notice it varying from book to book.
The τέλειος word group (mature/perfect/complete) is thematic in Hebrews and recurs in Paul, Matthew and James, and needs a coordinated policy on “mature” versus “perfect.”
The noun and its verb range over encouragement, comfort, exhortation and appeal across Acts, Paul and Hebrews, and translations vary widely for the same sense.
It recurs across the letters as “patience,” “longsuffering” or “forbearance” and needs to be kept distinct from ὑπομονή (“endurance”) consistently.
It occurs in Mark 7:4, Hebrews 6:2 and 9:10 and Colossians 2:12 (variant), and a single decision is needed on “washings” versus “baptisms” and on its distinction from βάπτισμα.
